subject: Clarifying billing when context length crosses pricing bands
messages:

Cc: Daniel Park <daniel.park@acmehealth.com>
Date: Wed, 14 Apr 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Question on rounding/discount when context crosses billing slab

Hi Marissa,

Thanks for the SOW draft — Daniel and I reviewed it and have one technical billing question before procurement signs: if a single conversational request (including history) pushes a call from one context band into the next (for example, the live model call grows from ~8.2k tokens to ~12.3k tokens because of appended history), how will that be charged against our committed discounts and minimums?

Specifics we care about:
- Do you meter the exact token count and invoice that raw number (i.e., 12.3k tokens), or is there any bucketing/rounding to the band boundary that would change how the committed-tier discount applies?
- If a single user session frequently hops between bands, do we see per-call rounding (and if so, to what quantum) or an aggregated monthly reconciliation?
- Does prefix/KV cache reuse reduce billed tokens in ways that affect whether a call is considered 'in-band'?

Attached: sample usage export and our proposed SOW redlines.

We want to make sure the economics in the SOW match our forecast model before moving to legal. Happy to hop on a quick call.

Best,
Sofia Ramirez
Senior Product Manager, Acme Health
sofia.ramirez@acmehealth.com

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Question on rounding/discount when context crosses billing slab

Hi Sofia — thanks for the clear examples and for sending the sample export. Short answer up front: we meter and invoice on actual token usage per request, then apply negotiated price/discounts at billing time. However, there are three important practical details that drive what you’ll see on invoices and in forecasts — I’ll outline them and include a short worked example below.

1) When we meter: tokenization happens at request time (input + output). The raw token count is what our metering emits. There is no silent promotion of a call to a higher "band" pricing tier in-flight — the per-token usage is what gets recorded.

2) Rounding & quantum: for synchronous (non-streaming) calls we round usage to the smallest billing quantum agreed in the contract (default: 1 token; many enterprise deals opt for a 100-token quantum for smoothing). For streaming calls we use a streaming cadence quantum (default: 10-token windows) because of the per-chunk accounting.

3) Discounts & committed tiers: your committed tier (monthly committed token amount in the SOW) determines the per-token price applied at invoice time. We first sum raw metered tokens across the billing period, apply any minimums/commit thresholds, then apply the negotiated per-token discount (or slab pricing) to the aggregated usage. Put simply: we don’t change the raw meter to "fit" a slab; we meter raw then apply price logic to the total.

Worked example (based on your scenario):
- Single call: actual tokens = 12,300 (after tokenizer).
- Contract quantum: 100-token rounding for planning (example only). Call rounds to 12,300 -> stays 12,300 (already a multiple of 100 in this simplified example).
- Monthly: if you used 3M tokens total, pricing tier breakpoints are applied to the 3M aggregate (e.g., first 1M at $X, next 2M at $Y), and then your committed discount is reconciled against that aggregate spend.

KV/prefix reuse: we do not double-charge tokens that are served from a live in-memory KV cache — the prefix is only billed the first time it is materialized into the request. However, for metering we treat cached tokens that are referenced in a response differently depending on whether they are transmitted (counted) to the client — if the model references them but does not emit them in the output tokens, they are not billed as output tokens.

Next steps: Karthik / Grace — can you confirm the default quantum values and whether we should propose 100-token quantum for Acme in the SOW? Sofia — I can sketch a short one-page billing playbook that maps common call patterns in your export to the expected invoice lines so procurement has a model to plug into their forecast.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Director, Revenue Strategy | Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com

We’d like the playbook you mentioned — that will make it easier to plug into our financial model. Also — can Redwood commit to a one-month pilot with a small usage credit so we can validate invoicing against our telemetry before the start of the committed term?

—Sofia

Subject: Re: Question on rounding/discount when context crosses billing slab

Thanks — good questions. Quick answers then actions: 

1) Rounding vs. discount order: rounding is a metering step (we round each call per the contract quantum), then we aggregate rounded metered tokens across the billing period. Discounts/tiers are applied to the aggregated number. So the rounding can slightly affect which slab buckets your aggregate usage lands in, because the invoice is computed from the sum of rounded call counts. We disclose the quantum in the SOW so there are no surprises.

2) KV/cache warmups: warmup activity is charged as normal metered usage by default. For large migrations or obvious one-time warmups we do two options on a case-by-case basis: (a) issue a one-time credit (common for pilot phases or migrations) or (b) exclude identified warmup jobs from the monthly reconciliation if mutually agreed in writing. We typically recommend option (a) for pilots.

3) Pilot credit: happy to propose a one-month pilot with a usage credit equal to the first ~200k tokens (or a negotiated amount) to validate invoices vs your telemetry. If that works we’ll add a pilot addendum to the SOW.

Attached: redwood-billing-playbook-v1.md (contains 3 examples mapped to invoice rows using your sample export), and a short pilot addendum template.
